preamble: Change of the voiced dental fricative [ð] to the alveolar tap [ɾ]. Old Literary Finnish had a weak-grade fricative [ð] (spelled d or dh) as the consonant-gradation partner of t. It was lost from most dialects, and its reflex varies by region: in South Ostrobothnian and in much of Tavastia it became r, so standard tahdon 'I want', uuden 'new (gen.)' and padan 'pot (gen.)' correspond to dialectal taharon, uuren and paran. Intervocalically this r is usually a single tap, although a full trill also occurs. Tavastian dialects also show an older l reflex, and eastern dialects show other outcomes. Standard Finnish d is a later spelling pronunciation.

examples.note: Word-internally r stands where the standard language has d. The r is the direct spoken reflex of old ð; standard d is a spelling pronunciation.
From the dialect sentence 'Mä taharon uuren puukoon lahajaks' ('I want a new knife as a present').
The r reflex is widespread in Tavastian; the older Tavastian l reflex gives palan.
Beside l-dialect lehlen. Mustanoja & O'Dell (2007) found that intervocalic r in such positions is a single tap about 90% of the time.

sources: Mustanoja, L., & O'Dell, M. (2007). Suomen d ja r sosiofoneettisessa kentässä. Virittäjä, 111(1), 56. https://journal.fi/virittaja/article/view/40542
